chapters.title: Chapter 5: Where Kelly Breaks Down, and Putting It Together

lessons.title: Building Your Own Position Sizing Framework: Key Takeaways

children.text: This course started with two Zerodha traders running the identical edge to opposite outcomes. Everything since then has been building the machinery to explain exactly why, and to give you a repeatable process instead of a gut feeling. This closing lesson compresses that machinery into one checklist and one final worked example, start to finish.

body.title: Position sizing, start to finish
steps: Classify the bet: discrete win/lose, needing p and b, or continuous exposure, needing μ and σ (Lessons 1.2, 2.1-2.3)
Estimate p/b or μ/σ from real data, and compute the standard error, not just the point estimate (Lessons 1.2, 3.3)
Recompute f* using a conservative, lower-bound estimate instead of the raw point estimate (Lesson 3.3)
Apply fractional Kelly, weighing confidence in the inputs, ability to survive a drawdown, and how concentrated the bet is (Lessons 3.1-3.2)
If holding multiple correlated positions, size them jointly with Σ⁻¹μ, never by summing individual fractions (Lessons 4.3-4.4)
Convert the fraction into actual lots or shares, always rounding down (Lessons 2.4, 4.1-4.2)
Check for Chapter 5's common failure modes: stale volatility, uncoordinated correlated adds, doubling down after losses, and an aging backtest (Lesson 5.1)
Remember the model's own assumptions can fail: fat tails, regime change, and correlation breakdown all argue for extra caution (Lesson 5.2)
Consider capping the result at whatever a simpler, μ-free method like volatility targeting would allow (Lesson 5.3)

children.text: A Quick Worked Pass, Start to Finish

A fresh example, run through the checklist without re-deriving anything: an Infosys swing setup, backtested on 95 signals, winning 45% of the time, with an average win of ₹120 per share against an average loss of ₹60 per share, on a ₹5,00,000 account.

body.caption: Every step of the checklist, applied once

body.text: 17.50% down to 1.25%, a 14-fold reduction, before the position is even converted into shares. This exact pattern showed up in Lesson 3.3's Bank Nifty example (21.25% to 2.84%) and Lesson 4.1's spread example (20.00% to 2.05%). It is not a coincidence specific to any one system; it is what honestly accounting for estimation error and drawdown risk does to almost every raw Kelly number this course has computed.

children.text: What to Do When You're Not Sure

There will be trades and positions where this framework's inputs are genuinely uncertain: a new setup with too few trades to trust, a fast-moving market where volatility has clearly shifted, a position that overlaps in ways that are hard to quantify with something else already held. When any of that is true, the default should be the more conservative of two answers: what Kelly-style sizing suggests after every discount in this lesson's checklist, or what a simple, μ-free method like fixed fractional or volatility targeting would allow. Never resolve genuine uncertainty by picking whichever method happens to justify the larger position.

body.text: Position sizing is not a footnote to a trading or investing strategy. It is the strategy that decides whether any edge you find ever survives long enough to compound into real wealth, or ends the account before it gets the chance.

body.title: One last diagnosis
body.scenario: You've found a new setup with a strong backtested win rate on only 40 trades. You're excited, and your gut says to size it aggressively while the edge is fresh.
body.prompt: Walk through which steps of the ten-step framework matter most here, and what they'd tell you to do.
body.modelAnswer: Step 2 matters most immediately: with only 40 trades, the standard error on the win rate is large, meaning the confidence interval is wide (recall Lesson 1.2's example: 30 trades produced a 37%-73% range on a 55% measured win rate). Step 4 follows directly: compute f* from a conservative, lower-bound estimate of p rather than the exciting raw number. Step 5 adds a second layer, since a system this new also scores poorly on "confidence in the inputs," one of the three factors from Lesson 3.2, arguing for quarter-Kelly or smaller rather than half-Kelly. The honest answer to "size it aggressively while the edge is fresh" is closer to "size it cautiously until the edge has proven itself on more data," not the reverse.

points: Position sizing, not just strategy selection, determines whether an edge translates into real growth or account ruin.

f* is only ever the start of a sizing decision: it needs a conservative discount for estimation error, a fractional-Kelly reduction for drawdown risk, correlation adjustment for multiple positions, and rounding down when converted into real lots or shares.
The gap between raw full Kelly and what should actually be traded is often large, frequently a ten-fold reduction or more, across very different systems and instruments.

Kelly's assumptions, stable parameters, no fat tails, a stable covariance matrix, can and do fail; fractional Kelly and periodic re-validation are the practical response, not a sign the theory was wrong.
When genuinely uncertain, default to whichever sizing method gives the smaller, more conservative answer, never the one that happens to justify the position you already wanted to take.
